about: Hleidr (Lejre on Zealand), the great hall at the head of the Roskilde fjord, 793 to 1066. Written 6 Oct 2026 from Design/content/dossiers/hleidr.md, the spine (threads riddle_road, godfreds_market, cross_and_grove, silver_road) and the chains riddle_trail, old_gods and reric_808. A draft for the user to overwrite. The ground gives halls, graves and silver with no names; the texts give names and are all later than 1012. Everything that leans on a late text says so, and (?) marks what is not verified. Woven into the region danes_norway on 7 Oct 2026 by the region's weaver: ties made to run both ways, people named in ties made real in their own ports or pointed at the right id, stories given beats and cards in the other ports, and the region's cards (encounters/danes_norway_793.json) named in the sites' 'do' lists.

ports.summary: Hleidr is a great man's hall on a rise among old mounds, an hour's walk inland from the head of a long shallow fjord on Zealand. It is not a town and has no market, no toll and no quay: a ship lies on the beach under the watch farm and her goods go up the stream valley on backs and carts to the steward's store. A merchant comes because a hall of two hundred mouths wants wine, glass, blades, querns and horses, and pays in weighed silver, hides, barley and captives, and because the men on its benches decide who is a guest in the Danish isles.
ports.seasons: The fjord has almost no tide: a hard west wind fills it and an east wind drains the landing, and in a cold winter the inner water freezes (?). The year turns on the hall's feasts, winter's start at the Winter Nights in the tenth month, Yule at midwinter, the offering for victory before the ships go out in spring, and on the autumn herring in the sound to the east.

history.text: About this year the first great hall is raised on the rise at Hleidr; four more follow on the same spot until about 1000.
history.source: Excavations of Tom Christensen, Roskilde Museum, 1986-1988, as given in en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heorot and da.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gammel_Lejre (dossier)

history.text: About this time a lord's man here wears a helmet with gilded bronze brows, of the kind buried at Valsgarde and Sutton Hoo. A piece of one is lost at the landing and another by the hall.
history.source: The Gevninge helmet fragment (found 2000, dated 550-700) and the Lejre eyebrow (found 2024, late 600s to mid 700s): en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gevninge_helmet_fragment; da.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gammel_Lejre

history.text: The Franks name Sigfred king of the Danes. No writer of his time says where he kept his hall.
history.source: Annales regni Francorum 777, 782, 798 (?); Design/content/realms/denmark.md. That Hleidr was his is not recorded.

history.text: The hall stands and is lived in. Nothing is written of it this year or any year near it.
history.source: dossier, section 5: no chronicle gives Lejre a year except 934

history.text: About this year a stone is cut and raised a half day's walk to the south-east: Gunnvald's stone, Hroald's son, reciter at Salhaugar. Three drinking horns are cut over the words.
history.source: The Snoldelev stone, Rundata DR 248 (runes_793.json snoldelev_dr248); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snoldelev_Stone; the date is usual and not sure (?)

history.text: Godfred, king of the Danes, comes with his fleet and all the horsemen of his kingdom to Sliesthorp, on the border of his land and the Saxons'.
history.source: Annales regni Francorum 804. The game keeps his household at Hleidr when he is not with the fleet (spine, thread godfreds_market): no source places him here (?).

history.text: Godfred is killed by one of his own following. Hemming, his brother's son, is king after him and makes peace with the emperor.
Hemming dies. Sigfred and Anulo fight for the kingdom and both are killed; the Franks hear that 10,940 men died in the battle.
About this year the hall is built new on the old spot.
history.source: Radiocarbon date of hall timber, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heorot (dossier)

history.text: About this year a smith casts a silver figure the height of a thumbnail: someone on a high seat with two birds on its arms.
history.source: The 'Odin from Lejre' figure, found 2 September 2009, 18 mm, 9 g: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odin_from_Lejre

history.text: In these years the dead of the hall are laid unburnt in the earth east of the houses, a few are burned, and stones are set over some in the shape of ships. One man is buried with gifts and a beheaded man laid over him.
history.source: da.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gammel_Lejre: 49 earth graves and 6 cremations of the 900s; the date of the ship settings is not given (?)

history.text: King Henry of the Saxons beats the Danes and makes their king take baptism. A German bishop writes eighty years later that Henry then forbade the great offering held at Hleidr every ninth year.
history.source: Widukind I.40; Thietmar of Merseburg, Chronicon I.17, by hearsay and not confirmed by any dig (dossier; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blót)

history.text: In the 980s King Harald, Gorm's son, founds a town with a wooden church of the Trinity and a king's house at Roskilde, across the head of the fjord from the landing.
history.source: Adam of Bremen II.28 (?); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roskilde. No trace of the church or the house has been found.

history.text: About the end of the 900s somebody at Hleidr puts four silver vessels, a weight, a silver disc and forty-four beads in a clay pot and buries it. Nobody comes back for it.
history.source: The Lejre hoard, found 1850, now in the National Museum, Copenhagen: da.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gammel_Lejre

history.text: About this year the last hall goes out of use. The seat of the Danish kings on Zealand is Roskilde.
King Cnut makes Roskilde a bishop's seat.
At Christmas Earl Ulf is killed in the church of the Trinity at Roskilde at King Cnut's word, after a quarrel over a game of tafl the night before.
history.source: The saga of Saint Olaf (about 1230, LATER) as given in en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulf_Jarl; the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle does not tell it

history.text: A warship thirty paces long, built at Dublin of Irish oak, is new this year. She ends her days sunk across the channel of this fjord at Skuldelev, with four others, after the game's years.
history.source: Skuldelev 2, felled 1042 (tree rings): en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skuldelev_ships. The sinking, about 1070 (?), is after 1066.

eras.text: A hall a hundred years old, patched and smoke-black, with a lord's following on its benches, craftsmen and farm people in the houses round it and old mounds on every skyline. Whose hall it is no writer says; the game lets the king of the Danes keep feasts here (?). Silver is weighed, never counted. Strangers are met at the beach before they are met anywhere else.

The king's hall when he is not with the fleet (the game's choice, with the spine; unrecorded). In 804 and 808 the benches empty for the muster and fodder, ale and bread are dear. After the killing of 810 Hemming keeps it for two winters; in 812 the hall is half empty of men, and the women know the count before the Franks do.

A quieter house. Kings are made and killed in Jutland and the hall feeds whoever holds Zealand that year. Pieces of the caliphs' coin and, from about 825, the small pennies of Sliesthorp come up the valley in purses, and are weighed like any other silver. The old hall leans; the feasts are kept.

A new hall on the old spot, the longest roof a Dane has seen. Men come home from England with silver and English words. Fine smiths work by the hall, the dead are laid in the earth east of the houses and stones are set over some of them in the shape of ships (?).

After the Saxon king's victory the great offering is no longer kept (so a German bishop says, long after). A king takes baptism in Jutland about 965 and the hall goes on as before, with a hammer under most shirts and a cross under a few.

The king builds a church and a house at Roskilde across the water, and the following goes where the king eats. The hall at Hleidr has a steward, a few old men and too many empty benches. Ships still land at the watch farm, bound now for the new town.

The hall is gone: post-holes under grass, a farm, the mounds and the stone ships. The landing serves Roskilde, a bishop's town from 1020, with a stone church building by the middle of the century (?). Knarrs from Norway and small coasters use the fjord. What the place was is a thing for old people's talk.

sites.name: The strand at the fjord's end
sites.see: A low shore of shingle and black weed at the head of a narrow bay, reeds to either side and alders behind. Three or four boats lie drawn up on rollers with their masts down; a ship's length off the water is knee deep. There is no tide to speak of: the wrack line shows where the last west wind left the water. It smells of mud, tar and wet rope, and geese go over all day.
sites.source: Lejre Vig, the southern end of Roskilde Fjord (da.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roskilde_Fjord); Gevninge as 'the port of Lejre' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gevninge_helmet_fragment); wind and not tide sets the level (Research/water_levels/baltic_east.md)

sites.name: The watch farm
sites.see: A long farmhouse and a byre on the first dry ground above the strand, with a turf bench against the south wall where a man can see the whole bay. A saddled horse stands tied by the door at any hour. There is no wall and no gate: only the path, which runs between the house and the midden, and the dogs. Peat smoke and horse.
sites.source: The farmstead at Gevninge, dug in 2000 and read as an outpost that anyone bound for the hall had to pass (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gevninge_helmet_fragment); the mounted watchman is our reading of it

sites.name: The slip under the alders
sites.see: A cleared patch east of the strand with a keel on blocks, split oak planks stacked and weighted to season, and a tar pot on three stones. A man and two boys work with axes; nothing here is sawn. Chips lie ankle deep and the smell of tar carries to the boats.
sites.source: Inferred (?): no yard has been dug at Gevninge. Boats of this water are known from the fjord itself (Skuldelev 3, a small Danish coaster of about 1040) and from the Gislinge boat on the Lammefjord to the west (story/ships_793.json built_at).

sites.name: The stream valley
sites.see: A cart track going south beside a small clear stream, wet meadow on one hand and oak wood on the other, crossing the water twice on flat stones. Pigs root under the oaks with a boy and a man watching them. On the rise ahead the hall roof shows over the trees long before the houses do, with round mounds to left and right of it.
sites.source: The way from Gevninge up the stream to the hall, some kilometres by land (dossier, section 1; the distance is the game's estimate); the swineherd of the king's estate is riddles_793.json r-gest-12

sites.name: The great hall
sites.see: A house as long as six ships laid end to end, its walls bowed like a hull, its roof carried on two rows of posts thicker than a man. Inside it is dark after the daylight: a long fire down the middle, benches along both walls, shields and hangings behind them, and the high seat halfway down the north side. It smells of smoke, wet wool, dogs and roast pork. A stranger is shown the low bench by the door.
sites.source: The halls at Mysselhojgard, mid 600s to about 1000; the length is given as 50 m by one account and 61 m by another, so no figure is used (dossier, section 2)

sites.name: The steward's store
sites.see: A sunken-floored house by the hall's east door with a plank roof and the only lock in the place. Inside are casks, sacks, bundled hides and a chest; outside, a trestle with a folding scale on it and a whetstone for trying silver. There is no market here. What the hall wants the steward buys at this door, and what it has too much of he sells.
sites.source: Inferred from the kind of place: goods came to such a seat as gifts, dues and plunder as much as by sale, and no market is recorded (dossier, section 4). A weight lay in the hoard of the late 900s.

sites.name: The brew-house
sites.see: A low house behind the hall with steam coming out under the eaves: a great kettle on stones, vats, a trough of sprouting barley, bunches of bog myrtle hung to dry. Women come and go with buckets. There is a bench outside where the hall's people sit when they want to talk without the lord hearing. It smells of malt, sweet and sour together.
sites.source: Inferred (?): a hall of this size brewed daily. Ale flavoured with bog myrtle, not hops, is the northern custom of these centuries (Design/content/economy/food.md).

sites.name: The cooking stones
sites.see: A grey heap as high as a man's chest beside the hall: stones cracked by fire and thrown out, generations of them, with split bone among them, cattle, pig and horse. A fenced yard lies behind it with one old post in the middle, dark and greasy at the top. On a feast morning pits are dug here and the meat goes in on hot stones. Crows wait on the fence.
sites.source: The heap of fire-cracked stones and bone beside the hall, read by the excavator as feast cooking or a place of offering (dossier, section 2, (?)); Lejre among the halls with a holy yard (Design/content/lore/gods_cult.md). The post is ours (?). Closed from 934 on Thietmar's word only.

sites.name: The smith's house
sites.see: A small house set apart downwind, with a clay hearth at knee height, a bellows of two goatskins and a stump for an anvil. Moulds of baked clay lie broken by the door. The smith works bronze, silver and iron as they come: a sword's hilt one day, a kettle's patch the next. Charcoal smoke, hot metal and the hiss of a quenching trough.
sites.source: Smiths and workers in fine metal by the hall (dossier, sections 2 and 3, from Christensen, marked (?)); the silver figure of about 900

sites.name: The great mound
sites.see: A round grass mound west of the hall, steep enough that sheep graze it sideways. It is the youngest of the big mounds and the only one whose dead the hall still names. A flat stone lies at its foot, stained by ale. From the top the fjord can be seen as a line of light to the north.
sites.source: Grydehoj, a cremation mound of the 600s with a thick layer of ash and gold thread among the remains (da.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gammel_Lejre; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lejre)

sites.name: The old rise
sites.see: A grassed swell of ground a little north of the hall where the horses are turned out. Old people say the first hall stood here, and in a dry summer the grass shows two rows of darker rings where its posts were. The young men of the following wrestle, race horses and throw dice here, out of the steward's sight.
sites.source: Fredshoj, the halls of the 500s and 600s, gone by 793 (dossier, section 2). The marks in the grass are ours (?).

sites.name: Salhaugar
sites.see: Half a day's walk south-east: two low mounds by a farm, and against the nearer one a seat of flat stones facing the yard. An old man sits there with a horn in his lap and a boy to lead him. Three horns interlocked are cut on the door post. Larks, wind in barley, and far off the sound of someone splitting wood.
sites.source: The Snoldelev stone, DR 248: 'Gunnvald's stone, Hroald's son, reciter at Salhaugar'; Salhaugar is taken to be Sallov by Snoldelev, about twelve kilometres from Lejre (?) (Design/content/chains/riddle_trail.md). The seat is invented.

sites.name: The stone ships
sites.see: A sloping field east of the houses with low stones set in the outlines of ships, bows to the south, the largest longer than the hall. Between them the turf is broken by newer graves. On a clear evening the shadows of the stones make the ships look as if they are under way.
sites.source: The grave field of the 900s and the ship settings, the largest 70 to 80 m long (da.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gammel_Lejre); their date within the Viking Age is not known, so they are shown from 900 only (?)

sites.name: The king's new town across the water
sites.see: An hour's row east from the strand, on a slope above a spring-fed cove: a wooden church with a shingled roof and a bell that carries over the water, a king's house beside it, and booths going up along the shore. It smells of new-cut oak. This is not Hleidr and the people of the hall say so often.
sites.source: Roskilde, founded by Harald Bluetooth in the 980s with a wooden church of the Trinity; a bishop's seat from 1020 (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roskilde). It is not a port of ports_793.json, so it is shown as a place reached from this landing. Never before 985.

people.name: Asgaut
people.trait: The steward of the hall: keeps the key, the scale and the seating, and has never in his life been hurried.
people.want: A full store before every feast, and nobody on the benches who was not asked.
people.fear: A winter when the king's following eats the hall empty and he must say so aloud.
people.voice: Slow and level. States what the hall needs as if it were the weather, and names a weight once.
people.looks: About fifty, tall and stooped, grey hair cut at the collar, a long brown tunic with a tablet-woven hem, a staff in one hand and an iron key the length of a hand at his belt.
knows: what the hall will take this month and what weight of silver it gives
who sits where and why
when the next feast is and who is asked
which lord's men are on the fjord

ties.note: His brother's widow. She runs everything he thinks he runs.
The skald seats himself above his place and the steward moves him down, every feast.
Trusts the watchman's word on a stranger before he has seen the stranger.
Speaks for the king to merchants from 804; the king does not speak to them himself.
Buys the hall's field hands of him on a tally and pays after harvest.
The carter at Ripa was a houseman here once and learned to keep a tally from him.
Takes the Vik chief's yearly gift on the king's behalf and weighs it in front of his man. It is as near to friendship as the two halls come.
Roulf of the isles carries for the hall from Ripa and is paid after harvest, like everyone.
The man who speaks for the strand at the Slie sends its takings on each winter, counted twice (?).

lines.greet: You came past the watch, so you are somebody's guest. Whose is still to be seen. What is in the boat?
lines.greet_again: The Frisian with the small boat. Your last cask was good. The one before it was not, and I have not forgotten either.
lines.greet_friend: Sit down. There is a place for you on the long bench this time, and I chose it myself.
rumour: The hall drinks a cask in two nights when the following is home. I can count nights. So can you.
Querns. The women grind on stones their grandmothers wore hollow. A man with Rhine stone could name his weight here.
Half the benches are empty this year. I set the boards for all of them anyway. It is not my place to count the dead.
lines.saying: A guest should know which door he came in by.
lines.farewell: Go with the west wind or wait a week for it. The fjord does not care which.

people.source: invented; the steward of the hall is the actor of the chains riddle_trail (step 6) and old_gods (step 7); the name from Danish parts (names_placeholder.json)

people.name: Tola
people.trait: The hall's brewer and the keeper of its women's house: remembers every face that ever sat on the low bench, and what became of it.
people.want: Honey and good malt before the feasts, and word of the boys who left the hall and never sent any.
people.fear: A feast where the ale runs short. It has not happened in her time and it will be said of her forever if it does.
people.voice: Quick and warm, with a question at the end of most things. Calls grown men by what they were called as boys.
people.looks: Past forty-five, broad, red forearms, a linen head-cloth, a dark apron dress with two plain bronze brooches and a string of blue glass beads, a wooden ladle hooked in her belt.
knows: who in the hall is owed, angry or leaving
what honey, malt and salt fetch here
the true count of men home from any muster
Ravn as a boy on the low bench, and why he left

ties.note: Fed him when he was a hall boy; has waited some twenty-five years to tell him what the old man said after he left.
Her dead husband's brother. She lets him think the key matters.
Sends ale to Salhaugar every tenth day and the news with it.
The swineherd gets the spent malt for his pigs and she gets the first ham.
The ferryman on the Slie sat on the low bench in her first years; he still sends her eels.
Her honey comes from the farmer Hebbi in the woods beyond the sound, and she pays for it a year behind.
A namesake who sells ale by a well at Ripa. Guests carry greetings between them.
Roulf brings her malt from the west and carries her news home.

lines.greet: A Frisian. Do they brew where you come from, or only sell other men's? Sit, tell me what honey costs in the south.
lines.greet_again: You again, and thinner. Does nobody feed you on that boat? Here. Drink it before the steward sees.
lines.greet_friend: I kept the corner of the bench. Now, your wife, your boat, your debt, in that order. I want all of it.
lines.greet_ravn: That grey one in your boat. He had fair hair and too many answers when I last saw him. Does he still?
rumour: Twelve went to the muster from this bench and I have brewed for seven since. Nobody has told the steward. He can count cups.
The old man at Salhaugar asks after every ship. He is waiting for one man, and he will not say so.
The skald buys his riddles from a swineherd and sells them to the king. Do not tell him I said it.
lines.saying: Ale tells you what a man is. Morning tells you whether he knew it.
lines.farewell: Come back before the Winter Nights. I brew strong then, and I shall want to know how it went.

people.source: invented; the name is a short name of Danish rune stones (names_placeholder.json). Her tie to Ravn rests on the spine: Ravn was set the last question here as a young man.

people.name: Thorulf
people.trait: The lord's poet: vain, exact, and honest about words if about nothing else.
people.want: A hard riddle nobody on the bench has heard, and a guest clever enough to be worth beating.
people.fear: That the old reciter at Salhaugar will die with what he knows, and that people will then ask the skald for it.
people.voice: Never gives a straight name to a thing if two crooked ones will do. Laughs at his own turns before anyone else can.
people.looks: About thirty-five, slight, a red-brown beard combed to a point, a blue cloak a little too fine for him pinned with a ring of silver, ink-black fingers from cutting and blacking rune sticks.
knows: the hard riddles, at a price
the old kings of the hall as the songs have them: Ro and Helgi, and the open-handed Rolf
who in the north keeps which lay
what the lord thinks of a guest, by where he was seated

ties.note: Learned the lays at the old man's knee, and wishes fewer people remembered that.
The matter of the seat.
The pig riddle is the swineherd's and the skald has sold it twenty times.
They shared the low bench as boys. Ravn answered more; Thorulf stayed.
Trades riddles with the skald at Birka by any skipper who can carry a stick without reading it.
The Svear king's poet claims the older lays. Thorulf says older is not better and means the opposite.
Sat one bench higher than the ferryman on the Slie, and still corrects him by messenger.
From 813 he makes his verses for Godfred's son, and is paid in rings (?).
Paid the weaver at the river mouth in Skane for a ribbon with a riddle about eight feet, and knows she had the worse of it.
The poet on the Karmsund has heard his best line and calls it borrowed (?).

lines.greet: A man from where the land is lower than the sea. Good. You will know what I mean by a house that swims.
lines.greet_again: The wave-horse rider is back. Have you an answer for me, or only silver? I take both.
lines.greet_friend: Sit by me. The steward will move us both, and then you will have a story to carry south.
rumour: They say a king here once sowed gold on a field to stop the men behind him. I say he knew his pursuers.
Two brothers held this place once, in the songs: one took the land and one took the water. The water was the better half.
The hard ones cost twelve pennyweights. The one I cannot answer myself is not for sale. Ask your grey steersman about it.
lines.saying: A riddle is a gift you have to open with your own knife.
lines.farewell: Go well. Bring me a word I have not heard, from any tongue. I pay for those.

people.source: invented; 'the king's skald' of riddles_793.json (r-gest-34 for 12 d, and the stanzas of Vafthruthnir's lay in texts_793.json). The stories of Ro, Helgi and Rolf Kraki are from the Chronicle of Lejre (about 1170), Saxo (about 1200) and Snorri (about 1220): LATER, and told here only as 'in the songs'.

people.name: Toki
people.trait: The swineherd of the hall's estate: slow of speech, quick at sums, and proud of pigs.
people.want: Salt enough to lay down every beast killed at winter's start, and a boar of some other blood.
people.fear: Wolves in the oak wood, and a stranger who counts his herd better than he does.
people.voice: Talks to the pigs and the guest in the same tone. Counts under his breath while he listens.
people.looks: Around thirty, short and thick, mud to the knees, an undyed wool tunic and hood, a holly staff, a horn on a cord, a lean yellow dog at his heel.
knows: the riddle of the ten tongues and forty feet, which is his own
what a pig, a hide and a side of bacon fetch
every path from the strand that does not pass the watch
where things are thrown out behind the hall

ties.note: Spent malt for hams.
A small one, about who made the pig riddle. He will not let it go.
The watchman's sister's son.
The carter at Ripa, once a houseman here, takes the hall's spare hides down the drove road south (?).
A cousin over the sound who grazes an old market ground and gives away the same two verses.

lines.greet: Mind the sow. She has nine and trusts nobody. Are you for the hall? Then you want the steward, not me.
lines.greet_again: The boatman. I counted you last time. One of you, two feet. I got it right twice.
lines.greet_friend: Here, hold this one. No, by the hind legs. A man who can hold a pig can hold a price.
rumour: They say the Danes had a dog for king once. I have known worse lords. A dog comes when it is called.
Salt is short. If the killing comes at winter's start and the salt has not, half of this goes to the crows.
There is a path round the watch farm, by the alder carr. I did not tell you. The dogs know it too.
lines.saying: Count your pigs in the evening. In the morning there are always more or fewer.
lines.farewell: Go on, then. Shut the hurdle behind you.

people.source: invented; the swineherd of the king's estate who gives r-gest-12 (riddles_793.json; chain riddle_trail step 6). The dog king Raka is from the Chronicle of Lejre, about 1170: LATER, the tale may be older (dossier, section 7).

people.name: Skardi
people.trait: The watchman at the landing: courteous, unhurried and impossible to get past.
people.want: To know every keel on the fjord by her sail before she is in hail, and to hand the watch to his son.
people.fear: The one ship he lets up the valley that he should not have.
people.voice: Formal with strangers, as if reciting; plain with men he has passed twice. Asks the same three questions in the same order.
people.looks: About thirty-five, long in the leg, a clipped fair beard, a grey riding cloak, a spear with a worn ash shaft, and an old helmet with one gilded brow and a bare rivet where the other was.
knows: every ship that has come up the fjord this year, and her business
the channels, the shoals by the islands and where the deep hole lies
how the wind will set the water tomorrow
who may go up to the hall today

ties.note: Sends a rider ahead of every stranger; the steward knows your cargo before you reach the ford.
His sister's son, who he says should have been a horseman.
The dealer lands captives at night to dodge the lord's share, and Skardi has caught him twice.
In his last years the watch is kept for Godfred's sons.
Bard, a Vestfold skipper who lies here windbound most autumns and brings whetstones.
A cousin across the sound, the wright Sote at the comb makers' market, who takes Skardi's friends over the bar (?).
A man of the same byname weighs the king's due on the Wends' shore. Each is asked whether he is the other (?).

lines.greet: Stand off a moment. Who are you, whose men, and what brings a keel that small this far up our water?
lines.greet_again: The Dorestad boat. You know the questions, so answer them and I will send the boy ahead.
lines.greet_friend: No questions. Draw her up by mine. My wife has eels on, and the steward can wait an hour.
rumour: Three long ships went out by the islands at first light, no cargo, shields inboard. I did not ask where.
East wind tomorrow. The strand will be dry for a ship's length by noon. Lie afloat or lie a week.
My father's father lost the other brow off this helmet on this beach. I still look when the water is low.
lines.saying: A watchman who guesses is a host. A watchman who knows is a watchman.
lines.farewell: Keep the three islands to your left hand going out. The right-hand water looks deeper and is not.

people.source: invented; the outpost at Gevninge and its piece of a gilded helmet (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gevninge_helmet_fragment). The challenge on the beach is the custom the watch implies; no poem is named.

people.name: Hroald
people.trait: The reciter at Salhaugar: blind, patient, and the keeper of more words than any man on Zealand.
people.want: One person to hand the seat to who knows the difference between what he holds and what he does not.
people.fear: That it ends with him: that his son is dead and the boy he sent away will not come back.
people.voice: Very quiet, so that people lean in. Asks, never tells. Lets a silence stand as long as it likes.
people.looks: Near seventy, thin as a rake, white hair to the shoulders, eyes clouded white, an old blue cloak, a drinking horn with a bronze rim in his lap and a boy's hand on his arm.
knows: the riddles of the blind guest, all but the answer to the last
the lays of the old kings of this place
who set which stick on the road from Dorestad
what Ravn answered, and why it was wrong

ties.note: Set him the last question when he was young. Ravn answered it, which is the one wrong thing to do with it.
A good ear and no patience. The old man says so to his face.
Her ale and her news come every tenth day.
One of the bench: the ferryman on the Slie hands on his sticks.
Has never met him: a stick has gone to Dorestad by a Danish skipper, and an answer has come back (?).
A shipman of the Vik who sat on the low bench and gives the old man's riddles away, which is what they are for.
A sister's grandson at Ripa was given his name. The old man has never asked whether he deserves it (?).

lines.greet: A step I do not know, and a second I have not heard for a long time. Sit. Which of you speaks first?
lines.greet_again: The merchant. You walk more surely than you did. Have you answers, or more questions? Either will do.
lines.greet_friend: Give me your hand. Good. Now tell me a thing I do not know, and I will give you one back.
rumour: My son cut the sticks and I set them. He is in the new mound. The sticks are still on the road.
The skald will tell you he holds everything. Ask him the one about the ear. Watch his mouth.
A king asked me once what was said at the pyre. I said I did not know. He gave me this horn for it.
lines.saying: A keeper of words must know where his store ends, and not build past it.
lines.farewell: Go with the boy as far as the road. Come again while there is someone here to come to.

people.source: The name, the seat ('thul', reciter) and the place are real: the Snoldelev stone, DR 248, raised for his son Gunnvald about 800 (?). Everything else is invented, and agrees with the chain riddle_trail (the blindness, the son's death, Ravn's youth). Marked historical for the name only.

people.name: Soti
people.trait: The hall's fine smith in the years of the new hall: makes things smaller than anyone else can and will not explain them.
people.want: Quicksilver for gilding, clean silver, and a customer who does not ask what a thing means.
people.fear: His eyes. He holds work at arm's length now, and his arm is not getting longer.
people.voice: Mutters at the work, not at you. Answers a question about meaning with one about weight.
people.looks: Forty or so, bent at the neck, burn-pocked hands, a leather apron, a singed beard tied in a knot out of the way, a pair of fine tongs always in his fingers.
knows: true silver from bad by its sound on stone
what quicksilver, gold wire and niello cost and who has them
which great men have ordered what, and for whose grave
how to fit a northern hilt to a Rhine blade

ties.note: The town smiths at the Slie cast by the hundred from one model. He says it shows.
Gets his beads from Birka for the women's strings and sends back wire (?).
Antler for tool handles from Tonna, who sells at the river mouth in Skane; a season unpaid (?).
Of his mother's kin, three lifetimes back: the folding scale on his bench was Soti the caster's at Ripa, or so the kin say (?).

lines.greet: Do not stand in the light. What have you got? If it is quicksilver, shut the door and name your weight.
lines.greet_again: The southerner. Your silver rang true last time. Put it there. Not on the moulds.
lines.greet_friend: Look at this, then. Closer. No, closer than that. Nine pennyweights and it has two birds on it.
rumour: Everyone who sees it tells me who it is. Half say the High One. My wife says it is wearing her apron.
The men home from England pay in cut pennies with a king's head on. I melt the king. Silver is silver.
A Rhine blade with one of my hilts fetches twice the blade. The Franks hang men for selling them. Not my hanging.
lines.saying: Whoever sits in the chair, that is who it is.
lines.farewell: Shut the door after you. The draught spoils the gilding.

people.source: invented; the silver figure of about 900 with niello and gilding, whose dress has been read as a woman's (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odin_from_Lejre). Fire-gilding with quicksilver is the period's method. The Frankish ban on selling arms to Northmen on pain of death: Edict of Pitres, 864 (spine, thread swords_north).

people.name: Alli
people.trait: The last steward of the hall: keeps the boards scrubbed for a following that eats at Roskilde now.
people.want: To hand the hall's silver cups to a lord who will drink from them here, not melt them for a church across the water.
people.fear: The king's men coming with a list.
people.voice: Dry and tired, with flashes of the old ceremony. Says 'the king' for the old one and 'the son' for the new.
people.looks: Past fifty, heavy and slow, a white moustache, a good cloak gone thin at the shoulders, the great iron key at his belt and a small hammer on a thong inside his shirt.
knows: what is left in the store, and what the hall will sell cheap
who at Roskilde can be trusted and who counts for the bishop
the old feasts as his grandfather kept them, and when they stopped
the ground round the hall, foot by foot

ties.note: Will not take the king's stamped pennies by count, only by weight, and tells the moneyer's men why (?).
The priest of the new church across the water asked for the hall's cups for an altar. Alli set the dogs on him, politely.
Never met him: the king's father's men hold the list Alli is afraid of.

lines.greet: You want Roskilde. Everyone does. It is an hour's row east. Or you could sit, and I could find a cup.
lines.greet_again: The house from the south. Your grandfather's grandfather sat on that bench, they say. It was fuller then.
lines.greet_friend: Come in out of the wind. I have four cups left that are worth drinking from, and nobody to set them for.
rumour: The king has a bell over there now. On a still morning I hear it. On a still morning I shut the door.
Every ninth winter there was a feast here that my grandfather would not describe. The Saxons ended it. So I was told.
They will come for the cups. A church eats silver like a hall eats pork.
lines.saying: A hall is its benches. The roof only keeps the rain off them.
lines.farewell: Go to your new town. If you come back this way, knock loud. I do not hear the door as I did.

people.source: invented; whoever buried the four silver vessels and the weight at the end of the 900s (da.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gammel_Lejre). The ninth-year feast is Thietmar's hearsay (I.17) and is spoken of here only as a thing past and untold.

people.name: Marcward
people.trait: A Saxon priest of the king's new church across the water from the old hall: patient, practical, and used to being the only man in the room who is sure.
people.want: Silver for the altar, wax for it, and one of the old hall's people at Mass before he dies.
people.fear: That the king's faith is the king's only, and goes into the ground with him.
people.voice: Slow Danish with Saxon bones in it. Says the hard thing mildly and then waits.
people.looks: As first met, in his twenties: spare, tonsured, a plain dark habit, a birch broom in his hand as often as a book; in age white-haired, with a bishop over him and the same broom.
knows: who at the new town is baptised, and who only stands at the back
what the old steward across the water still holds, and what the king's word says of it
the feasts and fasts, and which the king keeps when he is here
which ships on the fjord carry Christians from the south

ties.note: asked the old steward for the hall's four cups for the altar, and was shown the dogs
signed the pilot with the cross when he was a boy on the king's isle, and is sent herring every Lent
prays for the king by name, and scrubbed his church floor after the Christmas of 1026
the moneyer at the Slie wanted the same four cups for his fire

lines.greet: You came up the old fjord and landed at the old strand, so you walked past a dead hall to find a living church. Most do it the other way now.
lines.greet_again: The merchant. Good. Sit. I hear confessions in three tongues and bad Danish, and yours I can follow.
rumour: The steward at the old hall has four silver cups and no lord to drink from them. I asked for them for the altar. He set his dogs on me. Politely, I grant him.
The people here say an old king named Ro founded this town. It was founded by a king named Harald, in my own time. I was there. Nobody believes me.
On a still morning our bell carries to the old hall. I am told the steward shuts his door. I ring it all the same.
lines.saying: A hall is its benches, the old man says. A church is its door, and ours is open.
lines.farewell: Go with God down the fjord. Keep the three islands on your left hand. The watchman's grandson told me that, and he is one of mine now.

people.source: invented: a priest of the wooden church of the Trinity that King Harald built at Roskilde in the 980s (Adam of Bremen II.28 (?); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roskilde); the priest of the story hleidr.pot_under_the_floor and of ahus.asgot's tie. Earl Ulf's killing in the church at Christmas 1026 is the saga of Saint Olaf (about 1230): LATER. Ro as founder is the Chronicon Lethrense and Saxo: LATER, and he says so. The name is Marcward (names_placeholder.json, Saxon)

stories.title: The low bench
stories.summary: Rune sticks 'from a guest' lead from Dorestad by Ripa and the Slie ferry up the long fjord to this hall, where the hand Ravn was set a question as a boy and answered it. The skald sells the hard riddles here; the one that cannot be bought is the old reciter's at Salhaugar, and he has been waiting for Ravn to come back and not answer it.
stories.picture: A dark hall seen from the bench by the door: a long fire, faces along both walls turned towards a grey-haired seaman standing, and at the far side a blind old man holding out a horn.

beats.text: A Danish skipper puts a rune stick into your hand, 'from a guest'. Ravn reads it and does not say whose cutting it is.
The ferryman on the Slie gives the next stick and lets slip that he once sat on a low bench in a hall on Zealand, beside a boy with too many answers.
Tola looks past you at Ravn for a long moment and says nothing to him. Later, alone, she tells you what the hall thought when he left, and that the old man never filled his place.
Below the hall the steward bars the path with his staff, and behind him Toki counts pigs. Answer the steward, drive the pigs, or give a guest's gift.
The feast. Thorulf sets his own riddle of the hawk and the duck across the fire, and a guest who cannot answer drinks the forfeit horn.
Hroald sits by his son's new mound. He asks what should be done with what he knows: a stone, an heir, or skins and ink.
For a house that learned at the Slie who sets the riddles: the old man at Salhaugar asks for the grey seaman to be brought up the path, to hear him not answer. (Sets rd_last_question.)
On the strand in the Vik another of the bench gives the first of three sisters away, and says who has the others.

endings.how: You helped raise the stone for Gunnvald and left the lore where it was.
endings.text: The stone is cut with two names, a seat and a place, and stands by the road. What the two men knew is not on it. Hroald dies in a winter soon after and the seat is not filled.
endings.reward: Sets ch_riddle_trail_end_stone; unlock_title_kings_guest_hleidr; about 800 d; Thorulf sells you the hard riddles at half weight for life.

endings.how: You had solved five riddles and brought Ravn, trusted, to stand before the bench.
endings.text: The question is asked again and Ravn says the one true thing: that no man knows. Hroald gives him the horn. Ravn sails with you while the old man lives, and Tola pours for the whole bench.
endings.reward: Sets rd_last_question and ch_riddle_trail_end_heir; unlock_title_kings_guest_hleidr, unlock_heirloom_thuls_horn, unlock_pilot_isefjord; about 1,400 d; rw_favour_hleidr; every person of the hall a fast friend.

endings.how: You paid for calfskin and a reader, and had the old man's lays written down.
endings.text: Five gatherings in an English hand hold what a Danish hall sang. Thorulf will not speak to you for a year. A churchman somewhere will one day ask who brought heathen songs to a minster.
endings.reward: Sets ch_riddle_trail_end_written and changed_norse_lore_written; the book as an heirloom; about 600 d; Hroald a fast friend, Thorulf wary.

stories.reward: The standing of a guest of the hall, the skald's hard riddles, and for the one who does it well, a horn, a pilot's knowledge of the fjord and a hall where every face knows the house.

stories.title: Four winters and two more
stories.summary: From 804 the king's household winters here when the fleet is in, and the hall eats what three halls would. The steward buys on a tally and pays when the king's share comes home: from the Wends' market in 808, from Frisia in 810. Then the king is dead by his own man's hand, Hemming keeps the hall two winters, and in 812 the tally is owed by men who are in the ground.
stories.picture: The steward at the store door at dusk, a split tally stick in each hand, behind him the long hall with every second bench dark and unlit.

beats.text: Asgaut wants wine, malt, salt and querns in weights he has never asked for before, and offers a split stick in place of silver: half now, half when the king's share comes in.
Ships are called out and nobody says where. The dealer Asulf is buying fetters. Skardi counts hulls and tells you, as a friend, to be somewhere else by midsummer.
The Wends' market, where Dragomir has a booth and the toll goes to the Danish king. What you saw on the strand at Hleidr is worth more here than any cargo, to him or against him.
Tola has the news before the hall does: the king is dead, cut down by a man of his own following. She is already brewing for a funeral feast nobody has ordered.
Hemming's hall: quieter, fewer horses, peace sworn with the emperor on the Eider. The steward honours the old tallies at two parts in three, or in full if you will wait.
Half the benches are empty. Asgaut lays out the split sticks of dead men on the trestle and asks what you will take for them: hides now, a place on the bench for good, or nothing.
The king is not at his hall: he lies on the heath by the Slie with every horseman he owns, and bread there is three times dear.
The chief in the Vik sends the hall a gift each year, which the steward weighs in front of his man. The chief calls it a gift. The steward calls it nothing, aloud.

endings.how: You carried on the tally through the king's winters and forgave the dead men's halves in 812.
endings.text: Asgaut burns the sticks on the long fire with the bench watching. From that night the house has a seat in the hall under whichever king holds it, and Godfred's sons know the name.
endings.reward: The unlock hleidr.guest_of_the_hall for the house and its heirs; counts towards unlock_title_danish_guest_right; standing in the Danish isles; Asgaut, Tola and Skardi fast friends; cast.horik easy from 813.

endings.how: You pressed the tallies and took payment in what the store still held.
endings.text: It is a fair cargo: hides, bacon, a few captives nobody claims. The steward weighs it out to the grain and does not ask you to eat. You are a merchant here, no more.
endings.reward: Goods worth about 700 d at Dorestad; no change in standing; Asgaut cool, Tola the same as before, because she expected it.

endings.how: In 808 you carried word of the ships to Dragomir at Reric before midsummer.
endings.text: Some booths at Reric are empty when the fleet comes. Skardi guesses who talked and does not say so. Asulf guesses too, and does.
endings.reward: Sets gf_reric_friend (and ch_reric_808_knows); cast.dragomir a fast friend; cast.asulf wary; Skardi cool for two years, then he asks you quietly how many got away.

stories.reward: A seat on the bench that outlasts kings, or a hold of hides and no welcome, or a friend among the Wends and a watchman who knows what you did.

stories.title: The bowl and the lot
stories.summary: A Danish skipper asks the house to the feast at winter's start. A Christian merchant on the low bench is handed a bowl of boiled horse with the whole hall watching, and the next morning an old man in a frosty yard lifts a slip of wood for anyone who puts a question and gives the water its share.
stories.picture: A wooden bowl coming hand to hand down a crowded bench by firelight towards a man with a cross on a thong, his steersman beside him staring at the floor.

beats.text: A skipper who knows your hand is loading for the islands. His lord keeps winter's start at Hleidr and the hall is short of drink: carry wine, come as a guest, or stay home.

beats.when: flag.ch_old_gods_5 and (month = 10 or month = 11) and year < 849
beats.text: Tola tells you how it goes before you go in: what is in the bowl, who watches, and that bread and ale passed on with a good word offend nobody who matters.

beats.when: flag.ch_old_gods_5 and not flag.ch_old_gods_7 and (month = 10 or month = 11) and year < 849
beats.text: The feast, from near the bottom of the bench. The bowl comes down the table. Eat what the hall eats, take bread and ale and pass it, or eat aboard with the steersman.
Morning, frost on the cooking stones. The old man who lifts the lots will ask the question for you if the water gets its share.
The priest of Saint Martin's has heard where you spent the Winter Nights. What you ate there matters more to him than what you sold.

endings.text: The bench makes room. Nobody at Hleidr asks again what you are. At Traiectum the priest sets you a fast of forty days and the story reaches Dorestad before you do.
endings.reward: Sets ch_old_gods_ate; the hall's people friendly at once; marten cheap here for a season; penance and cooler feeling among churchmen until it is done.

endings.how: You took bread and ale, said a good word, and passed the bowl on.
endings.text: Pride only. The steward notes it and does not mind; Tola says it was well done. You stay a stranger who knows how to behave, which is a thing of value here.
endings.reward: No cost; Tola and Asgaut feeling up a little; nothing for the priest to hear.

endings.how: You gave the water its share at the cooking stones the next morning.
endings.text: Forty pennies' weight of cut silver goes into the stream. The old man lifts a slip and tells you what it says. Ravn carries himself differently on the way down the valley.
endings.reward: Sets ch_old_gods_paid_sea; -40 d; a true price word for furs here; Ravn's trust; the vow counts as kept if it was made to the sea.

stories.reward: A place on the bench without a question asked, or a clean name with the priests: seldom both.

stories.title: Whoever sits in the chair
stories.summary: About the year 900 the smith Soti is casting something very small for someone very great, and needs quicksilver to gild it and black for the silver. He will not say who it shows. Fetch what he needs and you see it finished, and hear the hall argue about it for the rest of your life.
stories.picture: A burn-scarred hand holding a silver figure no bigger than a fingertip up to the smithy door's light: someone seated on a chair, two birds on its arms, four strings of beads on the breast.

beats.text: Soti shows you a wax model on the end of a pin and asks for quicksilver, an ounce or two, and sulphur for the black. He names a weight in silver that makes you look again at the pin.
Quicksilver comes to the Slie from the far south in sealed horn, by few hands. The town smiths buy all of it. One will sell if he does not know who it is for.
The bead makers at Birka have the small blue beads Soti's wife wants copied in silver on the figure's breast. She sent the count: four strings.
The figure is done. Half the hall says it is the High One with his ravens. Soti's wife says it is wearing her apron. Soti says: whoever sits in the chair, that is who it is.

endings.how: You brought the quicksilver and asked no questions.
endings.text: Soti cuts your house's mark under an anvil stump and from then on fits and gilds for you before any lord's man. The figure is lost in the grass within a lifetime and found in 2009.
endings.reward: The unlock hleidr.sotis_bench; a gilded weather vane or stem ornament for the ship at cost; Soti a fast friend.

endings.how: You brought it and pressed him to say who the figure was.
endings.text: He takes the quicksilver, pays the weight he named and shuts the door. You have a fair profit and an opinion, like everyone else.
endings.reward: About 300 d profit; Soti cool; a saying to carry: the chair, not the sitter.

endings.how: You sold the quicksilver to the smiths at the Slie for the better price.
endings.text: Soti gilds with what he can scrape together and the gilding is thin on one side. It still is, under glass.
endings.reward: About 450 d profit; sliesthorp.goldsmith friendly; Soti wary for good.

stories.reward: A fine smith who works for you first, and the sight of a small thing made that people will still be arguing over eleven hundred years on.

stories.title: Four cups and a weight
stories.summary: In the 990s the king's following eats at Roskilde and the hall at Hleidr has a steward and no lord. Alli holds the hall's last silver, four vessels, a weight and a string of beads, and men are coming to count it for a church. He asks a merchant he trusts what should be done with silver that has no hall.
stories.picture: An old man kneeling on an earth floor by a single lamp, lowering a clay pot into a hole, a silver cup catching the light at the rim; a merchant holding the lamp.

beats.text: Alli sets out four silver cups on the trestle, one of them of foreign work with beasts on it, and a lead weight cased in bronze. He asks what such things fetch in the south, and whether they must be melted to fetch it.
A priest at the Trinity church knows of the cups and has the king's word that the old hall's goods are the king's. He would rather have them given than taken.
At the Slie stamped pennies pass by count now and old vessels are bought for the pot. A moneyer's man will give weight for weight less a tenth, and ask nothing.
A night with a lamp and a spade. Alli has a clay pot and has chosen the place. He will tell you where, or not, as you ask.

endings.how: You held the lamp and did not ask to be told the place.
endings.text: The pot goes into the ground. Alli dies within a few winters and tells nobody. It lies there until a man digging in 1850 puts his spade through the clay.
endings.reward: Alli gives you the hall's second weight set: sets sv_scale if you had none; the unlock hleidr.old_weights; Alli a fast friend; your heirs are told at this landing that the house 'kept its mouth shut once'.

endings.how: You talked him into giving the cups to the Trinity church, and carried them over.
endings.text: Three become a chalice and a dish. The fourth, the one with the beasts, the priest keeps as it is. Alli never forgives himself, or quite forgives you.
endings.reward: History changed a little: no hoard is found in 1850. Standing with the king's men at Roskilde; act:audience at the new town opens; about 200 d as a gift from the church; Alli cool.

endings.how: You bought them by weight and sold them at the Slie.
endings.text: A good piece of business, and the end of the hall's table silver in a moneyer's pot. The steward weighs it out without a word and shuts the store.
endings.reward: About 900 d profit; the store closes to you; told against the house at this landing for a generation.

stories.reward: A dead hall's weights and its last friend, or the new town's favour, or silver.

works.name: A brushwood way through the wet valley
works.what: Bundles of hazel and alder laid across the two soft places on the track from the strand, pegged down and topped with gravel, with split logs at the stream crossings.
works.picture: Men laying bundles of brushwood across a bog in a line towards a hall roof on the skyline, a loaded cart waiting behind them.
works.needs: The steward's leave (friendly with Asgaut or his heir) and a dry month.
works.gives: Carts reach the hall in any weather: carrying up from the strand takes half the time and no porters are lost to the mud. The hall's people call it by your house's name.
works.source: Brushwood and plank trackways across wet ground are the north's ordinary road-making in these centuries (the Ravning Enge bridge of about 980 is the great example); none has been found on this path (?)

works.name: A shed on the strand
works.what: A long low house of posts and turf open at the seaward end, where a boat can be drawn in on rollers and lie dry through the winter with her gear.
works.picture: A boat's stem looking out of a low turf-roofed shed on a snowy shore, the fjord frozen grey behind.
works.needs: Leave of the watch farm (friendly with Skardi or his heir) and oak posts from the lord's wood.
works.gives: The boat may winter here safe from ice and thieves at no cost; goods may be stored at the landing (act:store); repairs on this strand take a third less time.
works.source: Boat sheds for wintering ships are known across the north in these centuries, best in western Norway; none has been dug at Gevninge (?)

works.name: A stone by the road for your dead
works.what: A boulder set upright by the track to the hall, with a line of runes cut and blacked: the name of one of your house, who set it, and after whom.
works.picture: A waist-high grey stone by a cart track, fresh-cut runes down its face, a carver kneeling with mallet and chisel and a boy holding a pot of black.
works.needs: A death in the house or the crew; a carver (the skald knows one); the lord's leave to raise it on his road.
works.gives: The house's name is read by everyone who walks to the hall: standing in the Danish isles; act:remember at the stone lifts the crew's heart; an heir is known here on first landing.
works.source: The Snoldelev stone of about 800 and the Gorlev stone of about 900, both near this place (runes_793.json snoldelev_dr248, gorlev_dr239)

works.name: A ship of stones
works.what: Low stones set in the grass on the grave field in the outline of a ship, bow to the south, over or beside a grave of your house.
works.picture: Two men with levers settling a boulder into a row that curves away like a ship's side, other stone ships in the long grass behind them at evening.
works.needs: A grave of the house here (act:bury), and a place on the field granted by the hall.
works.gives: The house is counted among the hall's own dead: the unlock hleidr.guest_of_the_hall passes to every heir without a gift; men of the hall hire to your ship before another's.
works.source: The ship settings on the Lejre grave field, at least four once (da.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gammel_Lejre); their exact date is not known (?)

ships.note: Four- and six-oared boats of the fjord, for eels, fowling and the run to the islands. One is always for sale on the strand; the watchman knows whose.
ships.picture: A slim six-oared clinker boat on rollers on a weedy beach, oars laid inboard, a farm on the rise behind.

ships.how: built to order over a winter
ships.note: A working boat of Zealand's inner waters, the same build as the one you came in. The wright under the alders can lay one down in autumn and have her tarred by the spring offering.
ships.picture: A short broad clinker hull half planked on blocks under bare alders, frost on the chips, a man fairing a strake with an axe.
ships.source: The Gislinge boat, found in the Lammefjord some 30 km west of here and built about 1130 (the game uses her build for the whole period: ship_classes_793.json gislinge; story/ships_793.json built_at)

ships.how: built to order over a winter
ships.note: The lord's oak and the lord's leave: a ship of twelve to fifteen paces that rows, sails and lands on a beach. Only a guest of the hall is sold one.
ships.picture: A long low ship with a single mast being run down a beach on rollers by twenty men, a steward with a staff watching from the bank.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json norse_allround_ship; story/unlocks_793.json unlock_ship_norse_allround_ship (hleidr); Skuldelev 3 for a small Danish ship of this water, about 1040

ships.note: Never sold. A man with the king's favour may be lent a warship and her crew for one season's voyage, for a share and an oath, when she is not wanted for the muster.
ships.picture: A long warship under oars leaving a narrow bay at dawn, shields inboard, a small merchant boat lying on the strand behind her.
ships.source: ship_classes_793.json norse_longship; raiders_793.json (Danes, home hleidr, from 800); the lending is the game's (?)

sayings.text: Within the gates ere a man shall go, full warily let him watch, full long let him look about him; for little he knows where a foe may lurk, and sit in the seats within.
sayings.source: Hávamál 1 (Bellows 1923; texts_793.json havamal_001; written down about 1270, older in substance)

sayings.text: Forth shall one go, nor stay as a guest in a single spot forever; love becomes loathing if long one sits by the hearth in another's home.
Cattle die, and kinsmen die, and so one dies one's self; but a noble name will never die, if good renown one gets.
Give praise to the day at evening, to ice when it is crossed, to ale that is drunk.
A guest should know which door he came in by.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner (the steward)

sayings.text: They made the king's poet sit below the salt-fish. He said the fish at least had been somewhere.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner: a Northman's understatement on the seating quarrel

sayings.text: The Franks count their silver and the Danes weigh it. That is why a Frank is rich on Monday and a Dane on the scale.
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; silver by weight north of the Eider (spine, thread silver_road)

sayings.text: A Frisian asked the watchman how deep the fjord was. 'To the knee,' said the watchman. 'Whose?' 'It depends on the wind.'
sayings.source: invented in the period's manner; the fjord's level is set by wind, not tide (Research/water_levels/baltic_east.md)

sayings.text: What did the High One say in his son's ear? If you know, you were not there; if you were there, you are not telling.
sayings.source: A turn on Gestumblindi's last question (texts_793.json t-gest-36; Vigfusson and Powell 1883); the turn is invented

easter_eggs.text: Skardi's helmet has one gilded brow and a bare rivet where the other was. At very low water a patient person can look for the lost one on the strand, and will not find it: it lay there until the year 2000.
easter_eggs.source: The Gevninge helmet fragment, a gilded bronze eye-piece of 550-700, found in 2000 (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gevninge_helmet_fragment)

easter_eggs.text: A stranger landing here is met on the beach by a mounted man who asks who he is, whose men he has, and what brings him. A poem made in England tells of just such a meeting on a Danish shore. Nobody here has heard it.
easter_eggs.source: The coast-guard of Beowulf, lines 229-257 (the poem names no place, and no Danish source names its hall: dossier, section 7). Kept as a quiet echo.

easter_eggs.text: The swineherd says the Danes once had a dog for king. The tale was written down at Roskilde some four hundred years after 793 by a clerk who also could not stand Germans.
'Gold is Kraki's seed', the skald says of the king who sowed it on a field. The by-name means a thin pole, given by a poor lad who was paid a ring for the insult and avenged the king for the ring.
easter_eggs.source: Snorri, Skaldskaparmal (about 1220) and Saxo (about 1200), as given in en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hrólfr_Kraki: LATER; told in the hall as old song only

easter_eggs.text: In a dry summer the grass on the old rise shows two rows of dark rings. Count them and pace them: a house of some fifty paces stood here two hundred years before yours did business.
easter_eggs.source: The hall of the 500s at Fredshoj, 48 by 11 m, found in 1997 (da.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gammel_Lejre)

easter_eggs.text: The largest of the old mounds is called a king's mound by everyone. It was a stone chamber raised by people who had no iron, older in 793 than 793 is now.
easter_eggs.source: The mound called Harald Hildetand's is a Stone Age chamber grave (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lejre)

easter_eggs.text: After 985 people at the new town say an old king named Ro founded it and gave it his name. Alli says it was founded last week by a king named Harald, and he was there.
easter_eggs.source: Ro as founder: Chronicon Lethrense and Saxo, LATER; the town is of the 980s (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roskilde)

easter_eggs.text: After 1042 a warship thirty paces long, built at Dublin, may be seen in the fjord. Her oak is Irish. She will lie on the bottom of this water for nine hundred years.

A German bishop will write that ninety-nine men and as many horses were killed here every ninth January. Ask anyone in the hall before 934 and they change the subject; ask after and they say their grandfathers never told them.
easter_eggs.source: Thietmar of Merseburg, Chronicon I.17 (about 1015), by hearsay, the numbers doubted and no dig confirming it (dossier, section 6). Never shown.

easter_eggs.text: On the door post at Salhaugar three drinking horns are cut, locked one in another. The same three are on the stone raised for the reciter's son, which stands today in Copenhagen.

unlocks.how: Call three times and answer Skardi's three questions truly each time, or give a gift at the watch farm once.
unlocks.gives: No waiting on the strand for leave to go up; act:lodge at the watch farm costs nothing; Skardi's word on tomorrow's water level before you beach (the grounding check at this landing passes as sure).

unlocks.what: The marks of the long fjord
unlocks.how: Be friendly with Skardi and sail the fjord in and out on five calls, or hire the pilot here twice.
unlocks.gives: Counts towards unlock_pilot_isefjord: no pilot's fee from the Kattegat to the strand, and the fjord may be run by night under a moon.

unlocks.what: A seat on the long bench
unlocks.how: End hleidr.kings_winters by feeding the hall, or hleidr.low_bench by any ending, or give at a feast (act:feast) in three different years.
unlocks.gives: act:audience and act:feast open at the hall without a gift; the steward buys from you before any other ship; the hall's men will not raid a hull known to be yours (flag unlock_title_kings_guest_hleidr where the chain gave it).

unlocks.how: Bring honey or malt to the brew-house on two calls, or bring Ravn to her once.
unlocks.gives: act:rumours here gives the true count of men home from any muster and the next feast's day; act:heal costs nothing; she speaks for you to the steward (haggle one step easier).

unlocks.how: Standing 'known' or better at the hall, and one riddle answered before the bench.
unlocks.gives: Thorulf sells r-gest-34 and the stanzas of the giant's lay (texts_793.json, Vafthruthnir) by weight; answer all he has and the favour rw_favour_hleidr follows (riddles_793.json).

unlocks.how: Be friendly with Toki, or bring salt to the hall before the Winter Nights.
unlocks.gives: act:buy_at_source in the valley: salt pork, hides and live pigs at the estate's own price in the tenth and eleventh months.

unlocks.how: End hleidr.chair_and_birds by fetching the quicksilver.
unlocks.gives: act:fit_upgrade at the smithy is done at cost and in half the days; a northern hilt fitted to any blade you bring raises its price in the north.

unlocks.how: End hleidr.pot_under_the_floor by holding the lamp.
unlocks.gives: A set of the hall's lead weights: sets sv_scale if the house has none, and act:weigh_silver cannot go against you anywhere in the Danish isles.
